### Supply Shocks and Peer Shocks in Corporate Finance {#sec-finance-shock-iv}

Corporate finance has its own instrument families, and they are rarely taught alongside the
labour economics canon even though the identification logic is identical. The recurring problem
is that a firm's financing, investment, and governance choices are jointly determined with its
prospects, and there is no lottery to appeal to. Three constructions do most of the work.

#### Within-Borrower Identification from Lending Supply

The cleanest of the three is @khwaja2008tracing. The question is whether a contraction in bank
lending supply causes firms to borrow less, and the obstacle is that banks and firms are matched:
banks that suffer liquidity shocks may lend to firms whose demand was falling anyway. A
cross-sectional regression of firm borrowing on the health of its bank confounds supply with
demand.

The design exploits firms that borrow from more than one bank. Differencing across two lenders of
the same firm in the same period removes anything at the firm level, including credit demand,
which is the confound. What remains is the difference in the two banks' liquidity shocks.

```{r finshock-km, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(202)

km <- function(nf = 800, nb = 60) {
  bshock <- rnorm(nb)                    # bank liquidity shock
  brank  <- order(bshock)
  fdem   <- rnorm(nf)                    # firm credit demand, unobserved
  # Assortative matching: firms with strong demand borrow from healthier banks.
  # This is what contaminates the cross-sectional comparison.
  pick <- function() {
    i <- round(rank(fdem) / nf * nb + rnorm(nf, 0, 8))
    brank[pmin(pmax(i, 1), nb)]
  }
  b1 <- pick(); b2 <- pick()
  keep <- b1 != b2
  b1 <- b1[keep]; b2 <- b2[keep]; fd <- fdem[keep]; n <- length(b1)

  L1 <- 0.8 * bshock[b1] + fd + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)   # true supply effect = 0.8
  L2 <- 0.8 * bshock[b2] + fd + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)

  long <- data.frame(L = c(L1, L2), shock = c(bshock[b1], bshock[b2]))
  c(cross_sectional = unname(coef(lm(L ~ shock, data = long))["shock"]),
    within_borrower = unname(coef(lm(I(L1 - L2) ~
                                       I(bshock[b1] - bshock[b2])))[2]))
}

round(rowMeans(replicate(200, km())), 3)
```

The cross-sectional estimate is roughly double the truth, because it credits the bank for lending
that the firm's own demand would have generated anyway. The within-borrower estimator recovers
0.8. The price is the estimand: it is identified only among multi-bank firms, which are larger
and better established than the population, and it differences out any aggregate contraction that
hits all of a firm's lenders equally. What survives is the relative effect of lender health, not
the total effect of a credit crunch.

#### Peer Firm Shocks

@leary2014capital ask whether firms imitate their peers' financing choices. The obstacle is
Manski's reflection problem in a corporate setting: firms in an industry share unobserved shocks,
so their leverage co-moves for reasons that have nothing to do with imitation. The instrument is
the idiosyncratic component of peer firms' equity returns, the part orthogonal to common factors,
which shifts a peer's financing choices without plausibly entering the focal firm's own leverage
equation. The design is the corporate analogue of the network instruments in
Section \@ref(sec-network-peer-iv), and it inherits the same objection: the exclusion restriction
fails if peer shocks propagate through product markets rather than only through imitation.

#### Flow-Induced Trading, and a Cautionary Tale

The third construction uses mutual fund flows. When investors redeem from a fund, the fund sells
its holdings for reasons unrelated to the prospects of any particular stock it holds. Aggregating
those forced sales across funds yields price pressure on a stock that is plausibly exogenous to
that stock's fundamentals. @edmans2012real use this to instrument for a firm's stock price and
estimate the effect of valuation on takeover activity.

The construction is attractive and it has been reused very widely, which makes
@wardlaw2020measuring essential reading before adopting it. The commonly used pressure measure
scales hypothetical forced trading by dollar trading volume. Dollar volume contains price, and
price is what the return is computed from. The measure is therefore mechanically related to the
outcome, and most of its variation comes from the denominator rather than from the flows the
design is supposed to be exploiting. The following makes the mechanism concrete.

```{r finshock-mechanical, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(303)

mech <- function(n = 3000) {
  ret  <- rnorm(n)                        # the outcome: pure noise here
  # Forced trading in a fire-sale sample is one-directional, so the numerator
  # does not average to zero across stocks.
  flow <- rnorm(n, mean = -1, sd = 0.3)   # exogenous, independent of ret
  # Dollar volume contains the contemporaneous price, so it moves with ret.
  volume <- exp(0.7 * ret + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5))

  c(scaled_by_volume = cor(flow / volume, ret),   # the common measure
    scaled_by_shares = cor(flow, ret))            # predetermined scaling
}

round(rowMeans(replicate(400, mech())), 3)
```

There is no causal relationship anywhere in this simulation. The return is independent noise, and
the flow is drawn independently of it. Yet the volume-scaled measure correlates with returns at
about 0.62, entirely because the denominator contains the outcome and the numerator does not
average away. Scaling the same flows by a quantity fixed before the outcome is realised, such as
shares outstanding, leaves the correlation at zero.

This is not a subtle weak-instrument issue, it is a construction defect, and no first-stage
statistic or overidentification test will reveal it. The lesson generalizes past this literature:
whenever an instrument is built as a ratio, the denominator is part of the exclusion restriction.

#### Practice

1.  Write the instrument down as a formula and check every term in it for the outcome. A
    denominator that contains price, return, or volume when the outcome is a price, return, or
    volume is disqualifying.
2.  Prefer scaling by a predetermined quantity: shares outstanding, lagged assets, lagged
    employment.
3.  For within-borrower designs, say explicitly that the estimand is relative and that it is
    identified off multi-lender firms. Do not present it as the aggregate effect of a credit
    contraction.
4.  For peer-shock designs, address product-market spillovers directly. A peer's idiosyncratic
    shock is excluded from the focal firm's financing equation only if it does not move the focal
    firm's own investment opportunities.
5.  Run the design on an outcome it should not affect. These instruments are usually strong enough
    that a placebo failure is informative rather than merely underpowered.
